{{Short description|Form of mathematical model}}
{{Orphan|date=February 2024}}
{{one source |date=April 2024}}
A '''tape diagram''' is a rectangular visual model resembling a piece of tape, that is used to assist with the calculation of [[ratios]] and addition, subtraction, and commonly multiplication. It is also known as a divided bar model, fraction strip, length model or strip diagram.{{fact|date=February 2021}} In [[mathematics education]], it is used to solve [[word problem (mathematics education)|word problems]] for children in elementary school.<ref>{{cite book |author1=Lisa Watts-Lawton |author2=Colleen Sheeron |title=Eureka Math Curriculum Guide: A Story of Units, Grade 2 yes |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=r5IvCgAAQBAJ&pg=PA128 |year=2015 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-1-118-81261-7 |page=128 }}</ref>

== Example ==

If, for example, a boy has won fifteen games, and the ratio of his wins to losses is 3:2, a tape diagram can be used to determine his number of losses, such as by doing

{| class="ckckck m 
| 
| style="background: #ccccff;" | 15
| style="background: #ccfcff;" | ?
| style="background: #ffffff;" | &nbsp;
|-
! colspan="4" | Total games lost = ?
|}
{| class="ckckck m 
| 
| style="background: #ccccff;" | 3
| style="background: #ccfcff;" | 2
| style="background: #ffffff;" | &nbsp;
|-
! colspan="4" | Total games lost = ?
|}
Since the ratio between his wins and losses is 3:2, and he has won fifteen games, it can be concluded that the boy has lost ten of these games.
